questions.content:
Industrialisation and its impact

(a) Describe two reasons why Britain was the first country to industrialise. (4 marks)

(b) Explain two ways in which industrialisation changed living and working conditions in British towns during the nineteenth century. (4 marks)

Total: 8 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] First reason identified, e.g. abundant coal and iron ore, a large colonial empire supplying raw materials and markets, or available capital from trade and banking.
[1] Developed with accurate detail, e.g. coal fuelled steam engines such as those improved by James Watt; cotton came from colonies and plantations.
[1] Second, different reason identified, e.g. an agricultural revolution freeing labour, good canals and ports, or political stability and a patent system.
[1] Developed with accurate detail, e.g. enclosure and new farming methods pushed people to towns; Britain's ports and canals moved goods cheaply.
(b)
[1] First change identified, e.g. growth of overcrowded towns such as Manchester and Birmingham.
[1] Explanation, e.g. migrants from the countryside lived in cramped back-to-back housing with poor sanitation, which spread diseases such as cholera.
[1] Second change identified, e.g. factory work replaced domestic work.
[1] Explanation, e.g. long hours, strict discipline, dangerous machinery and child labour, later limited by laws such as the Factory Act of 1833 and the Public Health Act of 1848.
Accept other accurate, relevant points. Common errors: placing the Industrial Revolution in the 20th century; confusing it with the later industrialisation of Germany or the USA.

questions.content:
Imperialism in Africa

Source A: a newspaper column (an imagined column written for this paper, by a fictional European journalist, 1890s)

Our nation has a duty to the peoples of the African interior. We carry railways, schools and medicine to lands that have known none of them. It is true that the new colonies also supply us with rubber, cotton and minerals for our factories, and that other powers are eager to claim what we leave behind; to hesitate now would hand our rivals both the prestige and the profit. A flag raised over a distant river is a sign of a great nation.

Source B: a letter (an imagined letter written for this paper from a council of elders in a fictional West African kingdom to a colonial governor, 1900s)

Our people did not ask for your railway, and we did not agree to your boundaries. Your tax collectors demand money that our farmers do not have, and our young men are taken to build your roads without pay. We were told that you came to help us. We ask the governor to let our own councils judge our own disputes, as our ancestors did, and to stop the forced labour.

(a) Identify two motives for imperialism that are given in Source A. (2 marks)

(b) Compare the attitudes towards colonial rule shown in Source A and Source B. Refer to both sources. (3 marks)

(c) Explain how the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885 affected Africa. (3 marks)

Total: 8 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] A motive identified from the source, e.g. a civilising mission (railways, schools, medicine) or economic gain (raw materials such as rubber, cotton, minerals).
[1] A second, different motive, e.g. rivalry and prestige (not letting other powers claim the land).
(b)
[1] Similarity or difference identified, e.g. Source A presents colonial rule as a benefit and a duty, whereas Source B presents it as imposed and harmful.
[1] Support from Source A (e.g. 'duty', 'railways, schools and medicine') and from Source B (e.g. tax, forced labour, boundaries not agreed).
[1] A developed comparison point, e.g. both mention infrastructure or labour but judge it differently; Source A sees a gift, Source B sees an imposition. Award this mark for an explained difference in perspective linked to the writers' positions (a colonial supporter versus the colonised).
(c)
[1] The conference, held in Berlin and hosted by Germany's chancellor, set rules for claiming African territory, such as effective occupation.
[1] It encouraged a rapid 'Scramble for Africa', with European powers dividing the continent.
[1] No African leaders took part, and borders were drawn with little regard to existing peoples and kingdoms, creating lasting divisions and conflicts.
Accept other accurate, relevant points. Common errors: stating that the conference began the slave trade; saying Africans were represented.

questions.content:
The First World War: the Somme

Source C: a letter (an imagined letter written for this paper by a fictional British soldier to his sister, dated 30 June 1916)

We have been told that the guns have been firing at the German lines for a week and that nothing can be left alive in front of us. Tomorrow we go over the top. The sergeant says the wire will be cut and we shall walk across. I have written this in a dugout that is damp and full of rats. Many of the lads are singing to keep their spirits up, though a few sit silently and write their last letters. Please do not worry, and tell Mother that I am not afraid.

(a) Identify two details from Source C about the conditions or feelings of soldiers before the attack. (2 marks)

(b) Analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying soldiers' experiences of the Battle of the Somme. Refer to its origin, purpose and content. (6 marks)

(c) Describe one reason why the Allies launched the Somme offensive in 1916. (2 marks)

Total: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] One detail, e.g. a damp dugout with rats; soldiers singing to keep spirits up; some men silently writing last letters; belief that the bombardment had destroyed the wire.
[1] A second, different detail.
(b)
[1] Origin: a private letter from a British soldier to his sister, written on the eve of the attack on 30 June 1916.
[1] Purpose: to keep in touch with and reassure his family, so he may hide his fear ('do not worry').
[1] Value: first-hand and written before the attack, so it shows what soldiers expected and believed, such as trust in the bombardment.
[1] Value: it shows a mix of emotions (singing, silence, fear) that official accounts often leave out.
[1] Limitation: it is the view of one ordinary soldier from one unit, so it cannot show the experience of the whole army, and he may not know the wider plan.
[1] Limitation: it ends before the attack, so it tells us nothing about what actually happened on 1 July; it may also be censored or softened to protect the reader. Award credit for a developed, supported judgement of overall usefulness.
(c)
[1] A reason identified, e.g. to relieve pressure on the French army at Verdun, or to break the stalemate on the Western Front.
[1] Developed with accurate detail, e.g. Verdun had been under German attack since February 1916; the offensive was a joint British and French plan along the River Somme.
Accept other accurate, relevant points. Common errors: placing the Somme in 1915 or 1918; naming it as a naval battle.

questions.content:
The interwar period

(a) Describe two effects of the Wall Street Crash of 1929 on Germany. (4 marks)

(b) Explain why many Germans resented the Treaty of Versailles of 1919. (6 marks)

Total: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] First effect identified, e.g. American banks recalled loans made under the Dawes Plan of 1924.
[1] Developed, e.g. German businesses failed and factories closed.
[1] Second effect identified, e.g. mass unemployment.
[1] Developed, e.g. around six million people were out of work by 1932; this increased support for extreme parties such as the Nazis and the Communists.
(b)
[1] The war guilt clause (Article 231) made Germany accept blame for the war.
[1] Reparations were set at 132 billion gold marks in 1921, seen as impossible to pay.
[1] Germany lost territory, e.g. Alsace-Lorraine to France and land to the new Poland, including the Polish Corridor.
[1] Germany lost all its overseas colonies.
[1] The army was limited to 100,000 men, with no air force and few warships.
[1] Germany was not invited to the negotiations and the treaty was called a 'diktat' (dictated peace).
Accept other accurate, relevant points. Common errors: stating that the treaty was signed in 1918.

questions.content:
Genocide and human rights

Source D: a diary entry (an imagined diary written for this paper by a fictional teacher from a Jewish family in a German city, 10 November 1938)

I walked to the school this morning and found the windows of the shops along our street smashed and the glass lying across the pavement. The synagogue was burning and the fire engines stood by only to protect the neighbouring buildings. Last night many men were arrested and taken away. Nobody can say where. Our neighbours looked away as I passed. For the first time I am afraid that there is no future for us here.

Source E: an extract from a leaflet (an imagined leaflet written for this paper by a fictional human rights group, 1947)

The world has seen what happens when the hatred of a people is turned into state policy. Words such as 'murder' do not describe the destruction of whole groups. The nations must agree on a law that names this crime and commits them to prevent it and to punish those responsible, wherever it takes place.

(a) Identify two actions against Jewish people in Germany that are described in Source D. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why the United Nations adopted the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in 1948. Use Source E and your own knowledge. (4 marks)

(c) Using both sources and your own knowledge, discuss how far the international community has protected human rights and prevented genocide since 1945. (4 marks)

Total: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] An action identified, e.g. shop windows smashed; the synagogue burned; men arrested and taken away.
[1] A second, different action.
(b)
[1] Context: the Holocaust, in which the Nazi regime murdered about six million Jewish people, along with millions of others, had shocked the world.
[1] Source E shows a belief that existing words and laws did not describe or cover the destruction of whole groups.
[1] The term 'genocide' had been coined in 1944, and the Nuremberg trials of 1945 to 1946 had shown gaps in international law.
[1] The convention was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 9 December 1948 to commit states to prevent and punish genocide (a day before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights).
(c)
[1] Support for success: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (10 December 1948), international courts such as the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and for the former Yugoslavia, and later the International Criminal Court (established 2002).
[1] Support for limits: genocide was not prevented in Cambodia (1975 to 1979), Rwanda (1994) or Srebrenica (1995), where UN forces did not stop the killings.
[1] Use of the sources: Source D shows the persecution that preceded 1945; Source E shows the aim to prevent such crimes, but the aim did not always become action.
[1] A reasoned judgement, e.g. important legal progress but weak enforcement because states acted by self-interest and the Security Council could be blocked by veto.
Common errors: dating the Convention before 1945; stating that Kristallnacht (9 to 10 November 1938) was the start of the mass murder in death camps.

questions.content:
The Cold War: the Cuban Missile Crisis

Source F: a newspaper report (an imagined report written for this paper by a fictional journalist of a neutral country, 28 October 1962)

The world has drawn back from the brink. After thirteen days in which many feared war, the Soviet leader has announced that the missiles in Cuba will be dismantled and sent home. The American president had ordered a naval quarantine of the island and warned that an attack from Cuba would be answered in full. Observers say that both leaders now have good reason to speak to one another more directly. Many ordinary people in this country spent the week listening to the radio in fear.

(a) Identify two events in the early Cold War, between 1947 and 1955, that increased tension between the USA and the USSR. (2 marks)

(b) Analyse the purpose and value of Source F for a historian studying the outcome of the crisis. (4 marks)

(c) Explain why the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 was a turning point in the Cold War. (4 marks)

Total: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] An event, e.g. the Truman Doctrine (1947), the Marshall Plan (1947 to 1948), the Berlin Blockade and Airlift (1948 to 1949), the formation of NATO (1949), or the Warsaw Pact (1955).
[1] A second, different event.
(b)
[1] Origin/purpose: a report for a newspaper written by a journalist from a neutral country, aimed at informing the public as the crisis ended on 28 October.
[1] Value: written at the time, it shows the public fear and the relief at the announcement, and it names the key actions (naval quarantine, dismantling of missiles).
[1] Limitation: written on the day the announcement was made, so it does not include the secret deal, the removal of US Jupiter missiles from Turkey, or the role of private diplomacy.
[1] Limitation or balance: a journalist writing for the public may simplify events and reflect the neutral country's fear of war. Award the mark for a supported judgement of overall value.
(c)
[1] It was the closest the superpowers came to nuclear war, with the world fearing a conflict from 16 to 28 October.
[1] It showed the danger of miscommunication, leading to the Moscow-Washington hotline in 1963.
[1] It led to the Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 and later talks on limiting nuclear weapons, beginning the period of detente.
[1] The Soviet withdrawal weakened the Soviet leader's position at home, and Cuba stayed communist under the US promise not to invade.
Accept other accurate, relevant points. Common errors: dating the crisis in 1961 or 1963; stating that the USA invaded Cuba.

questions.content:
Decolonisation

(a) Describe two ways in which the Second World War weakened the European colonial empires. (4 marks)

(b) Explain why the partition of British India in 1947 led to violence. (4 marks)

Total: 8 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] First way identified, e.g. European powers were left economically exhausted and in debt after the war.
[1] Detail, e.g. Britain relied on American loans and could not afford to defend its empire.
[1] Second way identified, e.g. nationalist movements were strengthened.
[1] Detail, e.g. Japan's early victories in Asia had shown that European powers could be defeated; colonial soldiers who fought for the Allies expected more rights; the USA and the USSR opposed old-style empires.
(b)
[1] India and Pakistan became independent on 15 August 1947 after Britain left the subcontinent.
[1] Borders, drawn quickly by the Radcliffe Line, divided the provinces of Punjab and Bengal, which had mixed communities.
[1] Millions of Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims crossed the new borders in fear, among the largest forced migrations in history.
[1] Existing religious tensions and mistrust between communities, and weak policing, led to massacres in which hundreds of thousands died.
Accept other accurate, relevant points. Common errors: dating independence in 1945 or 1950; saying Gandhi was Prime Minister.

questions.content:
The civil rights movement in the USA

Source G: a newspaper editorial (an imagined editorial written for this paper for a fictional Northern city newspaper, December 1955)

In a Southern city, thousands of Black residents have refused to ride the city buses after a local seamstress was arrested for declining to give up her seat to a white passenger. They walk to work, share cars and meet each evening in churches to plan the next day. There is no violence in their protest, only quiet determination. The bus company has begun to lose money, and the city leaders must now ask themselves how long they can defend a rule that so many find unjust.

Source H: a memory (an imagined recollection written for this paper by a fictional participant in a march, recorded years later)

We left our town before dawn on a chartered bus. When we reached the capital in August 1963, the crowd was so large that I could not see the end of it. There were Black and white people, young and old, churches and unions together. We sang, we listened to the speeches, and we went home believing that the nation could no longer ignore us. I remember feeling that we were part of something bigger than any of us.

(a) Identify two methods of protest described in Source G. (2 marks)

(b) Compare Source G and Source H as evidence of the methods and aims of the civil rights movement. (4 marks)

(c) Explain how the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 changed the position of African Americans. (4 marks)

Total: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] A method, e.g. a boycott of the buses, walking or car-sharing, or meetings in churches.
[1] A second, different method, including non-violent protest.
(b)
[1] Similarity: both describe peaceful, organised mass action (a boycott and a march) aimed at ending racial injustice.
[1] Difference: Source G describes a local protest in one city aimed at ending segregated buses; Source H describes a national march aimed at drawing the attention of the whole country.
[1] Supported by evidence from each source, e.g. 'quiet determination' and economic pressure in G; 'a crowd so large' and unity of Black and white people in H.
[1] Evaluation of nature of the sources: G is a contemporary outsider's opinion written for readers in the North, while H is a later personal memory which may be affected by hindsight. The March on Washington on 28 August 1963 supports the details in H.
(c)
[1] The Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlawed segregation in public places such as restaurants, hotels and theatres.
[1] It banned discrimination in employment on grounds of race, colour, religion, sex or national origin.
[1] The Voting Rights Act of 1965 banned literacy tests and other barriers used to stop Black citizens voting, and allowed federal oversight in places with a history of discrimination.
[1] Black voter registration rose sharply in the South, though discrimination in housing, jobs and policing continued.
Accept other accurate, relevant points. Common errors: confusing the Acts with Brown v Board of Education (1954); dating the Acts in the 1950s.

questions.content:
The end of the Cold War

'The Cold War ended mainly because of the economic weakness of the Soviet Union.'

To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your answer, consider the economic weakness of the Soviet Union and at least two other factors, and reach a supported judgement about which factor was most significant. (12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Clear position on the extent of agreement, made in the introduction.
[1] Economic weakness: the Soviet economy was stagnant and heavy military spending, estimated at a large share of national output, could not be sustained.
[1] Specific detail, e.g. shortages of consumer goods, falling oil prices in the 1980s and the cost of the war in Afghanistan (1979 to 1989).
[1] Gorbachev's reforms: perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness), introduced from 1985, weakened the control of the Communist Party and encouraged criticism.
[1] His decision not to use force to keep control in Eastern Europe (the end of what is sometimes called the Brezhnev Doctrine) allowed change in 1989.
[1] Pressure from the West: the US arms build-up under Reagan and the Strategic Defense Initiative (1983) increased the cost of competition.
[1] Opposition and nationalism: Solidarity in Poland (legalised in 1989), peaceful revolutions in Hungary, East Germany and Czechoslovakia, and the opening of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989.
[1] Nationalist movements in the Baltic and other Soviet republics led to the dissolution of the USSR in December 1991.
[1] Analysis of links between factors, e.g. economic weakness made reform necessary, and reform released the opposition.
[1] Counter-argument fairly considered, e.g. weakness alone does not explain the timing or peaceful nature of the end.
[1] Judgement about the most significant factor, supported with evidence and a reason why the others are less important.
[1] Communication: a structured, balanced response with accurate use of terms and dates. Award this mark for a clear, organised argument.
Indicative content only; accept other valid factors and arguments. Common errors: stating that the Wall fell in 1991 or that Reagan alone ended the Cold War.

questions.content:
Extended response

'The twentieth century was shaped more by the violence of war and genocide than by the struggle for freedom and human rights.'

Evaluate this statement. Support your answer with specific evidence from at least three of the following: the First World War, the interwar period, the Second World War, the Cold War, decolonisation, the civil rights movement. (16 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] A clear thesis in the introduction that answers the question and defines the key terms (violence of war and genocide, struggle for freedom and rights).
[1] Argument for war and genocide: the First World War caused around ten million military deaths and ended four empires (German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman).
[1] The Treaty of Versailles and the Great Depression linked to the rise of dictators and the Second World War (1939 to 1945).
[1] The Holocaust and mass killing in the war showed the extreme of state violence.
[1] The Cold War shaped global politics through alliances, nuclear weapons and proxy wars (e.g. Korea 1950 to 1953, Vietnam).
[1] Argument for freedom and rights: decolonisation after 1945, e.g. India 1947, Ghana 1957 and Algeria 1962, gave self-determination to millions.
[1] Civil rights in the USA, e.g. the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 to 1956, the March on Washington in 1963 and the Acts of 1964 and 1965.
[1] The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) and the Genocide Convention (1948) were responses to violence, linking the two themes.
[1] Evidence is accurate and specific (dates, names, events), with at least three different periods or events used.
[1] Analysis of links, e.g. war weakened empires and thereby encouraged decolonisation; the Holocaust led to human rights law.
[1] A counter-argument is considered, e.g. struggles for freedom were often made possible or necessary by war, or violence itself came from denial of rights.
[1] Evaluation of the significance of different developments, with reasons (scale, duration, long-term effects).
[1] A judgement that is supported rather than only asserted, e.g. that war changed the structure and rights movements changed the values.
[1] Clear, logical organisation with paragraphs and links back to the question.
[1] Precise historical vocabulary used correctly (e.g. appeasement, nationalism, self-determination, segregation).
[1] A conclusion which follows from the argument and weighs both sides.
Indicative content only; accept other valid arguments and evidence. Credit organisation and clear communication under criterion C. Common errors: narrative without evaluation; dates and names in the wrong order.
